## Proof

**The answer is No.** Surjectivity of $H_1(q,\mathbb{Q})$ does **not** force the fiber cardinality $|q^{-1}(x)|$ to be constant over all $x\in X$.

### Key observation

For a covering map $q:Y\to X$, the fiber cardinality $|q^{-1}(x)|$ is **locally constant** on $X$ (by definition of a covering map: every point of $X$ has an evenly covered neighborhood with a fixed number of sheets). Hence it is constant on each connected component of $X$, but it may differ between different components. The question is therefore only meaningful when $X$ is disconnected, and there the $H_1$-surjectivity condition is too weak to enforce global constancy.

A useful general fact: for any **finite-sheeted** covering of a path-connected base, $H_1(q,\mathbb{Q})$ is automatically surjective. Indeed, the transfer (corestriction) associated to an $n$-sheeted covering gives a homomorphism $\tau:H_1(X,\mathbb{Q})\to H_1(Y,\mathbb{Q})$ satisfying
$$
q_*\circ \tau \;=\; n\cdot \mathrm{id}_{H_1(X,\mathbb{Q})}.
$$
Since $n\neq 0$ in $\mathbb{Q}$, $q_*$ admits a right inverse $\frac1n\,\tau$, hence is surjective. So **every** finite-sheeted covering — regardless of the number of sheets — induces a surjection on $H_1(-,\mathbb{Q})$. The surjectivity condition therefore carries no information relating the sheet counts of different connected components of $X$.

### Explicit counterexample

Let
$$
X \;=\; S^1 \;\sqcup\; S^1, \qquad Y \;=\; S^1 \;\sqcup\; S^1,
$$
and define $q:Y\to X$ componentwise by
- $q_1:S^1\to S^1,\; z\mapsto z^2$ on the first component (a $2$-sheeted covering),
- $q_2:S^1\to S^1,\; z\mapsto z^3$ on the second component (a $3$-sheeted covering).

Since each component of $X$ is open-and-closed and $q$ restricts to a covering map on each, $q$ is a covering map.

**Fiber cardinality is not constant:**
$$
|q^{-1}(x)|=\begin{cases}2,& x\in \text{first }S^1,\\[2pt]3,& x\in \text{second }S^1.\end{cases}
$$

**$H_1(q,\mathbb{Q})$ is surjective:** Using $H_1(S^1,\mathbb{Q})\cong\mathbb{Q}$,
$$
H_1(X,\mathbb{Q})\cong \mathbb{Q}\oplus\mathbb{Q},\qquad H_1(Y,\mathbb{Q})\cong \mathbb{Q}\oplus\mathbb{Q},
$$
and the induced map is the direct sum of the component maps:
$$
H_1(q,\mathbb{Q}) \;=\; (\times 2)\;\oplus\;(\times 3)\;:\;\mathbb{Q}\oplus\mathbb{Q}\;\longrightarrow\;\mathbb{Q}\oplus\mathbb{Q}.
$$
Since $2$ and $3$ are both nonzero in $\mathbb{Q}$, this linear map is an **isomorphism**, hence surjective.

### Conclusion

We have produced a covering map $q:Y\to X$ such that $H_1(q,\mathbb{Q})$ is surjective (in fact an isomorphism), yet $|q^{-1}(x)|$ takes the values $2$ and $3$ on different components of $X$ and is therefore **not** constant. Hence the answer to the question is

$$
\boxed{\text{No.}}
$$

The underlying reason is that surjectivity of $H_1(q,\mathbb{Q})$ is guaranteed for every finite-sheeted covering (via the transfer, since the number of sheets is invertible in $\mathbb{Q}$), so it cannot constrain the sheet count across distinct connected components of the base.
